Reno, Nevada. October 10, 2026, about 2:30 p.m.

A woman and her husband were driving south on I-580, just past the Mill exit near the Grand Sierra Resort and the Reno airport, when she noticed a silver shape coming in from the east. She has lived in Reno a while and is used to the big training aircraft that pass through, so at first it didn't seem strange. "This was not that," she wrote in her report to the National UFO Reporting Center.

What she saw looked like two silver wings, swept slightly forward, with no fuselage at all, hovering motionless above the hills just east of the airport. She kept waiting for it to get larger on approach, or turn to line up with a runway. Neither happened. A moment later, "the craft fell straight down to the ground," dropping behind the hills and out of sight.

Her husband suggested a hovercraft, or something from an Air Force base out east. But she says she has seen her share of drones and never one shaped like a silver wing, and this one was "gigantic," much larger than a commercial aircraft. "It was the strangest thing I've ever seen."

About one minute, in broad daylight. NUFORC posted it as report 201552.

Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Fort Mifflin, Mud Island, built starting 1771.

Fort Mifflin sits on the Delaware River below Philadelphia, near the airport. In the fall of 1777, British forces laid siege to it, and the fort took the heaviest bombardment of the Revolutionary War. Of the roughly 406 to 450 men in the garrison, 250 were killed or wounded before the Americans pulled out on November 15. During the Civil War, it held Confederate prisoners along with Union soldiers and civilians.

Its most famous ghost is the Screaming Woman. Local lore names her Elizabeth Pratt, an officer's wife who disowned her daughter for falling in love with an enlisted man. The daughter died before they could make up, and the story says Elizabeth took her own life soon after. Witnesses claim her screams from the officers' quarters have been loud enough that police were called out to look for a murder.

Then there is the Faceless Man. Believers tie him to William H. Howe, a Union private convicted of desertion and the murder of an officer, who was held in solitary in a cell now known as Casemate 11 and hanged at the fort on August 26, 1864, in front of a crowd that had paid for tickets. The story says his ghost has no face because a bag was placed over his head before the hanging. "I think he's not at rest because he was made an example of," Fort Mifflin paranormal host Greg O'Brien told PhillyVoice. Some historians now argue Howe was unfairly treated, and O'Brien himself isn't sure the Faceless Man is Howe at all, since many soldiers lost their heads to cannonballs in 1777.

Here is the debate. Research published by Tony Selletti in Fort Mifflin: A Paranormal History found that Elizabeth Pratt never lived in the officers' quarters at all. The Ghost Research Society notes there are very few firsthand accounts of the Screaming Woman, and no proof the screams even come from inside the fort, since those quarters sit right at its edge.

Tomorrow night, October 24, Fort Mifflin locks its gates at 7 p.m. for an overnight ghost investigation that runs until 6 a.m.

Saw Mill City Road in Shelton, Connecticut, is a dirt road with a reputation. It's where the Melon Heads supposedly lurk.

Top 5 things to know about the Melon Heads:

1) The Melon Heads are a piece of American folklore from Ohio, Michigan and Connecticut, described as humanoids with large, bulbous heads who come out of hiding to attack people. In Connecticut, Saw Mill City Road in Shelton is the dirt road where they supposedly lurk, and the stories spread through towns like Trumbull, Monroe, Newtown and Stratford.

2) Connecticut tells two main origin stories. In one, an asylum for the criminally insane in Fairfield County burned down in the fall of 1960, and 10 to 20 inmates were never accounted for and fled into the woods. In the other, a Colonial-era family from Shelton and Trumbull was banished after accusations of witchcraft and retreated into the forest.

3) Many versions place the Melon Heads along a road called Dracula Drive. No town with the legend actually has a Dracula Drive. Instead, real roads get the name, including Saw Mill City Road in Shelton, Velvet Street in Trumbull and Monroe, and Edmonds Road in Oxford.

4) In Kirtland, Ohio, the story is about orphans in the care of a mysterious Dr. Crow, who supposedly experimented on them until they turned on him, burned the orphanage and ran into the woods along Wisner Road. Research suggests Dr. Crow likely never existed.

5) In Michigan, the Melon Heads are said to roam the woods around Felt Mansion after being turned loose from the Junction Insane Asylum. The Allegan County Historical Society says that asylum never existed, but locals have told the tale for decades, and one township manager said his friends called them "wobbleheads."

Garrettsville, Portage County, Ohio. March 6 to 10, 2026, revisited October 14, 2026.

For a few days last March, a rural corner of northeast Ohio became the most talked about place in the country for people who follow Bigfoot. Between March 6 and 10, a run of reported encounters around Mantua, Garrettsville and Windham, just east of Akron, was posted online, picked up by Fox News within days and later revisited by CNN, which called it "the Ohio Flap of 2026."

It started just after noon on March 6, when a researcher reported a brown figure about 120 yards away near State Route 44 in Mantua Center. The next night a witness said he saw an 8-foot figure near Mantua, heard heavy footsteps and a grunt, and found large muddy prints. On March 9, two witnesses described a face-to-face encounter, about 15 seconds long, with a 10-foot black figure on the Headwaters Trail near Hankee Road. A Windham resident who called themselves a longtime skeptic said, "I know what I saw, but I don't know what I saw." On March 10, a man in Newton Township let his German Shepherd out at 4 a.m. and the dog lunged toward the wood line, where he saw a huge black shadowy figure. By March 11, eight reports had been counted.

Almost every account came through one group, the Bigfoot Society podcast, and its host Jeremiah Byron said witnesses were "extremely shook up." The Portage County sheriff posted joke photos of Bigfoot being "arrested," and Garrettsville police said they had no calls at all. Skeptics point out that Bigfoot reports track black bear populations, that many witnesses were anonymous, and that a wave of fake reports followed. No photo, video or physical sample from the cluster has been independently examined.

Deadwood, South Dakota. Reported October 20, 2026.

The Adams House was built in 1892. It is named for W.E. Adams, who bought it in 1920 and went on to become one of Deadwood's richest and best known residents, the man who funded the Adams Museum. In 1934, Adams suffered a stroke and died shortly after, inside the home.

According to Black Hills Paranormal Investigations, the first hint that the house was haunted came from his second wife, Mary. The house was left to her, but she found she couldn't live there alone. She closed it up and moved to California. She still came back to Deadwood every year, but she stayed at the Franklin Hotel, not in her own home. When people asked why, she said the house was haunted.

Mary sold the house in 1987. It spent several years as a bed and breakfast, the city of Deadwood bought it in 1992, and after a restoration it opened as a museum in 2000. The stories never stopped. During its investigations there, BHPI staff say they heard what sounded like talking from empty rooms, footsteps coming up the stairs and whistling from other parts of the house. The group was first contacted by former Deadwood History executive director Mary Kopco, who claimed she had even seen the apparition of Adams himself.

This weekend, October 23 and 24, Deadwood History and BHPI are running the final round of their public paranormal investigations inside the house.

Bradshaw Ranch, outside Sedona, Arizona. First-hand account published October 19, 2026.

Alan Megargle, a community contributor for Atlas Obscura, says his night at Bradshaw Ranch started going strange on the road in. He was riding in a rented Jeep with his father-in-law Ron, his brother-in-law Joel and a guide who goes by Hoodoo Tall, who had been investigating the ranch for a few years. Hoodoo had driven that rough dirt road many, many times. This time he missed a turn, they came upon a house none of them had seen earlier that day, and he finally gave up. They found their way back with a phone GPS. They had planned to arrive at 9 p.m., and even after at least 50 extra minutes of driving around, they arrived at exactly 9 p.m.

At the ranch style house that Bob Bradshaw built after buying the property in 1960, the group tried a REM pod and a spirit box. Megargle says a ghost detector app on his phone locked onto a figure across the room. He walked toward it and pushed a K2 meter into it, felt a column of ice-cold air, and watched the meter spike and stay pegged until he pulled his hand back. Then the figure on his screen disappeared into the wall.

Their next stop was the old adobe building, which he calls the oldest standing structure in Sedona. When he stood up from the REM pod, he was facing southeast, looking straight out the window. About 50 feet away, a dark figure stood silhouetted against the night sky. He estimated it at about 6 feet tall and 4 to 5 feet wide at the shoulders, hunched over "like a linebacker." It moved to one side, then the other, getting closer each time, for almost 2 minutes. He says he couldn't speak or move until it was gone. They went outside and found nothing.

On the drive back, Hoodoo asked if he had seen his photo, a creature he says he photographed at the ranch a few months earlier. Megargle says it matched what he saw. "It was a Bigfoot."

It is one man's account, with no picture of his own sighting, and phone ghost apps are far from proof. But a lost road, a cold spot and a giant shape at the window is a lot for one night.

Cleveland, Ohio. Franklin Castle, 4308 Franklin Boulevard, built 1881 to 1883.

In Cleveland's Ohio City neighborhood stands a rock-faced sandstone mansion with a round corner tower, four stories, more than twenty rooms and eighty windows. German immigrant Hannes Tiedemann, a wholesale grocer who became a banker, built it from 1881 to 1883, back when Franklin Boulevard was one of the most upscale streets in the city. Today most Clevelanders know it as Franklin Castle, and it's often called the most haunted house in Ohio.

The legend grows out of the Tiedemann family's grief. Their daughter Emma died of diabetes in 1881 at age 15, and the stories say her ghost and her mother Louise's still wander the house. Around the time a German singing club sold the building in 1968, those rumors spread across Cleveland's west side. The family who lived there from 1968 to 1974 claimed the house was haunted, and one of them said she was warned the house was evil and that she should move out. After they left in 1974, the next owner offered public tours of "haunted" Franklin Castle. In 1975, a reporter was photographed exploring a hidden room behind a panel, and human bones turned up in a closet that same year.

Now the debate. Cleveland Historical points out that Emma died before the house was even finished, and that despite the rumors circulating since the 1960s, none of the Tiedemann children died in it. Like many families of that era, the Tiedemanns had lost three infant children to disease between 1863 and 1873, long before this house existed. The Encyclopedia of Cleveland History calls the haunted house stories spurious and says they don't seem to go back before 1965. And those bones? They're believed to have been planted by the owner to drum up publicity for his ghost tours. The rumored secret passages for Prohibition bootlegging don't exist either, apart from a small servants' stairway.

The house has had a rough run since. Michael DeVinko, Judy Garland's last husband, restored it and lived there for over a decade. Shortly after he sold it in 1999, an arsonist set it on fire, and in 2011 new owners bought it and kept restoring. Ghost hunters still come knocking, including Ghost Adventures in 2020. So is Franklin Castle haunted, or just a beautiful old house that got a reputation?

Source: https://clevelandhistorical.org/items/show/531

Birmingham, Alabama. Sloss Furnaces, 1882 to 1971.

For almost ninety years, the towering blast furnaces at Sloss turned out pig iron in the heart of Birmingham. The first blast was in April 1882, and the furnaces didn't go cold until 1971. Instead of letting it be torn down, Birmingham voters approved a $3.3 million bond in 1977 to save it, and in 1981 it became a National Historic Landmark, the only blast furnace in the country preserved and restored for public use.

Its best known ghost story actually started across town. On September 10, 1887, Theophilus Calvin Jowers, an assistant foundryman at Alice Furnace, was working around the edge of the furnace to loosen a bell when he lost his balance and fell with it into the molten iron. According to Alabama storyteller Kathryn Tucker Windham, he had once promised his wife, Sarah, "as long as there's a furnace standing in this county, I'll be there."

Later stories say workers soon saw him making his rounds, checking on his old crew. Others reported a male figure moving through spots far too hot for anyone to survive, or a sudden cold. When the first Alice Furnace came down in 1905, his ghost was said to turn up at a second furnace until it closed in 1927, and then to move across town to Sloss. In Windham's telling, his son John said he saw a ghostly figure striding through the hot furnace at Sloss from the 1st Avenue North Viaduct in 1927.

Here's where the debate comes in. Look up Sloss ghosts today and the name you'll see most is James "Slag" Wormwood, a brutal graveyard shift boss said to have fallen into the furnace in October 1906 and to haunt the place ever since. But according to Bhamwiki, Birmingham's local history wiki, Slag is a fictional creation, invented by the marketers of the Sloss Fright Furnace haunted attraction, which ran every October from 1998 to 2019. In 2022 the Sloss board decided the event didn't fit the landmark's mission, and it never came back.

So the real story may be stranger than the marketing: a ghost legend that seems to start with a real 1887 death, with a made-up villain stacked on top of it decades later. Is anyone still working the night shift at Sloss?

For more than a century, people in the mountains of western North Carolina have pulled over at dark overlooks and waited for the Brown Mountain lights to appear.

Top 5 things to know about the Brown Mountain lights:

1) The Brown Mountain lights are reported ghost lights near Brown Mountain in North Carolina, watched from spots like the Brown Mountain Overlook on NC Highway 181 near Jonas Ridge, North Carolina, Wiseman's View and Table Rock in the Linville Gorge Wilderness, and overlooks on the Blue Ridge Parkway.

2) The earliest published mentions date from around 1910 to 1912. A September 24, 1913 report in the Charlotte Daily Observer described red "mysterious lights seen just above the horizon every night," showing up "punctually" at 7:30 PM and again at 10 PM.

3) Locals asked their Congressmen for an investigation. In 1913, USGS employee D.B. Sterrett concluded the lights were Southern Railway locomotive headlights, and in 1922 USGS scientist George R. Mansfield used a map and an alidade telescope to show that the lights people were seeing were trains, car headlights and brush fires.

4) The legend kept growing anyway. A ghost story about a murdered woman and baby took in the lights in 1936, a claim of Native American lore first showed up in print in 1938 with no sources, and Scotty Wiseman's 1961 song "The Legend of the Brown Mountain Lights" made them the most popular ghost story in North Carolina.

5) Today they still draw ghost hunters and, since 2022, an annual Brown Mountain Lights Festival in Morganton. But low light cameras installed by Appalachian State University had logged 6,300 viewing hours by 2014 without recording a single unexplainable light.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Mountain_lights

In July 1952, radar operators watched unknown blips swarm over the White House and the Capitol in Washington, D.C., and fighter jets were sent up to chase them.

Top 5 things to know about the 1952 Washington, D.C. UFO flap:

1) From July 12 to 29, 1952, a wave of UFO sightings hit Washington, D.C., with the biggest nights on back-to-back weekends, July 19 to 20 and July 26 to 27. It became known as the Washington flap, the Washington National Airport Sightings, or the Invasion of Washington.

2) At 11:40 p.m. on July 19, air traffic controller Edward Nugent at Washington National Airport spotted seven objects on his radar, and senior controller Harry Barnes later wrote that "their movements were completely radical compared to those of ordinary aircraft." When objects moved over the White House and the Capitol, Barnes called Andrews Air Force Base, where an airman in the tower saw what looked like "an orange ball of fire, trailing a tail."

3) On July 26 the blips came back, and F-94 Starfire jets were scrambled from New Castle Air Force Base in Delaware. Lieutenant William Patterson chased four white glows, and according to Project Blue Book spokesman Albert Chop, he radioed, "I see them now and they're all around me. What should I do?" Nobody answered, Chop said, because nobody knew what to tell him.

4) Headlines like "SAUCERS SWARM OVER CAPITAL" ran across the country, President Harry Truman had his air force aide call Blue Book chief Edward J. Ruppelt for an explanation, and the Pentagon press conference on July 29 was the largest since World War II.

5) The Air Force blamed temperature inversions for the radar blips and misidentified stars, meteors and city lights for the visual sightings. Not everyone bought it. Former controller Howard Cocklin told the Washington Post in 2002, "I saw it on the [radar] screen and out the window."

In the summer of 1978, something big, hairy and walking on two legs kept coming back to one family's backyard outside Minerva, Ohio.

Top 5 things to know about the Minerva Monster:

1) The Minerva Monster is the name given to a Bigfoot-like creature reported in August 1978 along U.S. Route 30, just west of Minerva, Ohio, in Paris Township, Stark County, behind the Cayton family home, where an old abandoned strip mine gave way to dense woods.

2) It started earlier that month, when the Caytons' grandchildren ran into the house crying that they had seen a large hairy monster in the pit. The adults who went out to look described a creature covered in dark matted hair, about 7 feet tall and 300 pounds, with no visible neck. "It just stood there," Evelyn Cayton said.

3) On the night of August 21, family and friends on the front porch saw two pairs of yellow eyes by an old chicken coop. Headlights showed two cougar-like cats, and then a large hairy figure on two legs stepped in front of them as if to protect them. Minutes later it stood at the kitchen window, about four yards from the table, for close to ten minutes before it left.

4) Stark County Deputy Sheriff James Shannon arrived about five minutes after it was gone and said the lingering stench smelled like "ammonia-sulphur." Deputies searched the area on horseback and in jeeps and turned up only unusual but unsubstantiated footprints, and more sightings followed on August 22 and 23 and into September.

5) The bear explanation never settled it. The Ohio Division of Wildlife dismissed bears at the time, investigators said local law enforcement leaned on the bear story partly to keep vigilantes and hunters out of the woods, and when asked if she had seen bears, Evelyn Cayton answered, "No, not unless they were mutated."

Occoquan, Virginia. Reported October 19, 2026.

Thirteen years ago, the ghost of a little boy was reported at Puzzle Palooza, a puzzle shop at 408 Mill St. in Occoquan. There were flickering lights, doors opening on their own, and puzzles that were mysteriously solved, with their boxes rearranged. The puzzle shop is gone now. Some people insist the boy is not.

Local artist and psychic Rachael Bright bought the business in 2019 and opened her art gallery, Local Colour. She told InsideNoVa that the day after she moved in, she found one of her painting smocks stretched out across the doorway. The smocks were the last thing off the moving truck, and she had set them down and forgotten about them. The door was locked and alarmed, and when she asked the landlord, he couldn't explain it either. "Somehow it unpacked itself and ... stretched itself across the welcome mat," she said.

Bright says she has since seen and spoken to the ghost, a 7-year-old boy named Tad Loef. She says he told her he had a Dutch family and two younger siblings, and that his father came over from the Netherlands around World War II. Local records have not been able to confirm his story, but Bright believes him. She now runs ghost tours in town and keeps them age-appropriate for Tad.

He isn't the only one, she says. A Civil War soldier is said to keep walking up the stairs at the metaphysical shop 13 Magical Moons, and another spirit in the oldest house in Occoquan tells visitors about the town's divisions during the Civil War. Local baker Cindy Najera says Tad once asked her if she was a baker, and she still brings him sugar cookies at least once every two months.

None of it can be proven, and the main witness is a psychic medium who says she lives with doubt from others. But in a small town where shop owners leave cookies for a ghost, the story of Tad isn't going anywhere.

Bar Harbor, Maine. Saturday, October 3, 2026, 9:15 p.m.

A couple from Westbrook had driven up for a weekend at the KOA campground in Bar Harbor, just over the bridge from Trenton and Ellsworth. They love to camp and stargaze, and that night they were sitting by the water in complete darkness, looking at a crystal-clear Milky Way with not a cloud in the sky.

According to the report filed with the National UFO Reporting Center, the witness looked north toward the airport and saw what seemed to be a satellite, until it slowed, stopped and darted back the other way. Then both of them noticed a cluster of five or six bright lights making wild maneuvers. The lights didn't blink. They darted back and forth, stopped, and climbed so high they faded out of sight, then came back. Sometimes they came together and hovered close, "almost like they were mingling or interacting with each other," then took off from each other at crazy speeds, in unison.

What unnerved the witness most happened twice. As a commercial plane approached the airport, one of the lights dropped lower and followed it, staying behind it until it was close to landing, then darted back up into the sky. The witness wrote that if these were some kind of military drone, there would be no way they'd be allowed near a commercial plane like that.

They watched for about 25 minutes. "I am not a tinfoil hat type of person," the witness wrote, adding that their partner is extremely levelheaded. They were so bewildered they went back to the cabin, packed their bags and drove home that night.

NUFORC posted it as report 201445 on October 14. Drones and aircraft can't be ruled out from a written report, and the witness lists aircraft nearby. But lights trailing planes on approach are not something you forget.

Juarez Valley, Chihuahua, Mexico, across the Rio Grande from El Paso, Texas. October 2026.

Something is said to be killing chickens, roosters and rabbits in the farm country along the river, and Mexico's best-known UFO investigator says it is not any animal he knows.

Jaime Maussan, who has covered UFOs on Mexican TV for more than three decades, calls it "El Ser de Valle de Juarez," the Juarez Valley Creature. He described it to Juarez outlet NetNoticias.Mx on October 12 as a small, hairless, alien-like being. "It's a predator. I'm not saying it's extraterrestrial, but it is something scary," he said. "It has agility. It has intelligence. It walks on two feet. It appears human. It has a head like a human." According to the El Paso Times, Maussan claimed that witnesses have seen it, including a boy who watched it grab a chicken by the head and scramble up a tree. Maussan says he doesn't believe it would attack people.

His team says a camera trap recorded it in the Juarez Valley on October 14, between 7 and 8 at night, and on October 17 they showed images of a pale white shape climbing over a wall. The descriptions don't line up neatly. Portland, Oregon. Old Town, 1880.

In 1880, three successful lumber barons built the Merchant Hotel in what was then called the Old North End, a part of Portland with a rather questionable reputation. Today Old Town Pizza & Brewing sits in the original hotel lobby, and its order window is the old reception desk. Under the floorboards are basements that tours bill as the famous Shanghai tunnels, said to have been used to nab unsuspecting sailors and carry them to ships docked on the Willamette River.

The building also has a resident ghost. Her name is Nina, pronounced "Nigh-na." As the legend goes, she was a young woman sold into prostitution at the hotel. Traveling missionaries convinced her to share information in exchange for freeing her, and soon afterward she was found dead, thrown down the elevator shaft. Staff say she never left. Diners describe a presence behind them or a faint waft of perfume, and Nina is often reported in a black dress, watching people eat and wandering the basement below. Some even wonder if she carved her own name into the brick of the old elevator shaft, which is now the backdrop of a booth in the back.

Historians, though, say the tunnels themselves are the bigger ghost story. The Oregon Historical Society's Oregon Encyclopedia calls it a myth that has grown since the 1970s, with claims of a secret network running under the waterfront, 1,500 or more men abducted every year, and the whole thing hushed up to protect Portland's genteel reputation. Shanghaiing was real. A crimp would hand a drunk or drugged sailor to a ship's captain for a fee often called blood money, and it happened in West Coast ports until steamships ended it around World War I. But historians have found no evidence of any tunnel network built for it.

The tunnel legend seems to trace back to romanticized Sunday Oregonian stories by journalist Stewart Holbrook in 1933, several of dubious authenticity, and to Michael P. Jones, who in the 1970s said he had discovered long-hidden tunnels and started giving tours. The passages that do exist were mostly built to move goods from the docks into basements. As the encyclopedia puts it, "Those who tour the so-called shanghai tunnels today walk into a basement, not through any iniquitous tunnels." So if Nina still walks down there, she may be haunting a legend as much as a hotel.

Lake Lanier, northeast of Atlanta, Georgia. April 1958.

To most Georgians, Lake Lanier is a place for boats and summer weekends. With about 12 million visitors in a single year, it is one of the most visited lakes the Army Corps of Engineers runs anywhere in the nation. But for decades it has also carried a darker reputation. Legend has it the ghost of a long-dead woman roams the lake in a flowing blue dress, mysterious arms reach out for swimmers from the watery depths, and angry spirits call people home to submerged graves.

The most famous tale is the Lady of the Lake. According to the story, a Ford sedan carrying two women careened off a bridge in April 1958 and tumbled into the water, and some say the ghost of one of those women still wanders the bridge at night in a blue dress, lost and restless. Divers have their own stories. In 2017 longtime diver Buck Buchannon told local media, "You reach out into the dark and you feel an arm or a leg and it doesn't move." Others claim to hear church bells ringing from a sunken church far below.

So is the lake cursed? It was created in the 1950s by flooding whole valley communities, and some 700 families sold a total of 56,000 acres to the government. Army Corps of Engineers spokesman Cesar Yabor told CNN the Corps moved the marked graves, but it is likely some unmarked ones were inadvertently left behind. An old auto racing track near Gainesville still sits on the bottom. The church bells, though, he said are not possible, since no such structure was known to be left behind. Georgia's Department of Natural Resources counted 203 deaths in drownings and boating incidents between 1994 and October 2020, and Yabor says the lake's size and popularity feed the tall tales, while its high visitation rate also means more fatalities.

The real history under the water is darker than any ghost story. Part of the lake covers the former town of Oscarville, a small Black community, and in 1912 white mobs drove all 1,098 Black residents out of Forsyth County. Historian Lisa Russell, author of Underwater Ghost Towns of North Georgia, put it this way: "The real haunting in this story is how history has made it impossible to ignore what was done to the land in North Georgia."

Wilder, Kentucky. Bobby Mackey's Music World, 1978.

For decades, country singer Bobby Mackey's honky tonk in Wilder, Kentucky, was promoted as "the most haunted nightclub in America." Mackey bought the property in 1978, and he has said the site was a slaughterhouse before a roadhouse went up there, one that ran under several names, including The Brisbane.

The legends grew from there. Local legends call the place a "gateway to hell," complete with a claimed "portal to hell" and a basement wall whose water stains are said to look like human faces. The legends say several spirits haunt it, including Pearl Bryan, a 22-year-old pregnant Sunday school teacher from Greencastle, Indiana, whose headless body was found in 1896 about two and a half miles away in Fort Thomas, Kentucky. Two dental students were convicted of her murder and hanged in 1897, but one legend claims her killers were Satanists who cursed the site. Another tells of a pregnant dancer named Johanna who is said to have taken her own life in the 1940s after her father murdered her lover, a singer at the club. Mackey, his wife Janet and caretaker Carl Lawson appeared on Jerry Springer in 1991 and Geraldo in 1992, and Ghost Adventures featured the club in its premiere episode in 2008.

Then come the skeptics. Searches of property records, newspapers and court files found no evidence for the legends, and no link has ever been established between the club and Pearl Bryan's murder. Science writer Sharon A. Hill called the supernatural claims and the "portal to hell" unsubstantiated, noting that the stories picked up new details over decades of retelling. The Campbell County Historical and Genealogical Society says it is "highly unlikely" that Pearl Bryan's ghost haunts the place, and a Northern Kentucky Tribune reporter who took the two-hour tour twice wrote that nothing happened to suggest it was haunted.

In March 2024 the club closed, with plans to move temporarily to Florence, Kentucky, while a new building goes up on the old site, and the owners said the "portal" and the face-stained basement wall would be relocated too. The original building was demolished on December 10, 2024. Whatever was in that basement, it is apparently moving with the band.

Savannah, Georgia. 6 West Harris Street, March 1860.

On Madison Square in Savannah stands the Sorrel-Weed House, a Greek Revival mansion designed by architect Charles Cluskey for shipping merchant Francis Sorrel. In 1954 it became one of the first two homes in Georgia named a State Landmark, Robert E. Lee visited the family there, and the floating-feather opening of Forrest Gump was filmed from its rooftop. It is also billed as one of the most haunted buildings in Savannah, with ghost tours inside every evening.

The story told on many of those tours goes like this. Francis Sorrel carried on an affair with a young enslaved woman named Molly, kept in quarters above the carriage house. His wife, Matilda, discovered them and leapt from the balcony to her death in the courtyard, and a few weeks later, the tale says, Molly was found hanged in the carriage house. Visitors describe sudden nausea and a choking feeling in the basement, panic for no reason, and fully charged phone and camera batteries that are dead by the end of the tour. Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures and BuzzFeed Unsolved have all investigated the house.

Historians tell a different story. Francis Sorrel sold the house to Henry D. Weed on June 14, 1859, and moved his family next door to 12 West Harris Street. Matilda died on March 27, 1860, and a letter written that same day by family friend Charles C. Jones Jr. says she sprang from a window of her residence on Harris Street, "next door to the house which was the family mansion for so many years." No Sorrel family record mentions an enslaved woman named Molly, and an archaeological dig showed that a depression in the carriage house floor, rumored to be a grave, was really an old trash pit. Historians point out that even as fiction, the Molly tale reflects the very real abuse enslaved women suffered in that era.

So if something really does walk these halls, who is it? Savannah ghost author James Caskey has floated another answer: the house sits on or near the southern tip of the British earthworks from the 1779 Siege of Savannah, which many historians call the bloodiest hour of the entire American Revolution.

Have you ever wondered what the Star of Bethlehem really was?

Top 5 things to know about the star the wise men followed:

1) In the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 2, wise men from the East follow a star to Jerusalem, where King Herod's chief priests and scribes point them to Bethlehem in Judea, south of Jerusalem, and the star goes before them until it stops over the place where the child Jesus was.

2) Matthew is the only one of the four Gospels to mention the star or the Magi, and the Greek word magi there probably means astronomers or astrologers, which was awkward for an early Church that condemned astrology.

3) In 1614 German astronomer Johannes Kepler worked out that Jupiter and Saturn met in a series of three conjunctions in 7 BC, though modern calculations show the two planets stayed nearly a degree apart, so it would not have been much of a show.

4) Other theories include a strikingly close Jupiter and Venus conjunction on June 17, 2 BC, a comet or nova that Chinese and Korean stargazers watched for over seventy days around 5 BC, and astronomer Michael Molnar's double occultation of Jupiter by the Moon on April 17, 6 BC, which scientists, theologians and historians debated at the University of Groningen in October 2014.

Top 5 things to know about the creature some call the Arizona Bigfoot:

1) The Mogollon Monster is said to roam central and eastern Arizona along the Mogollon Rim, and cryptozoologist Don Davis claimed he saw it in the mid-1940s on a Boy Scout trip near Payson, Arizona, describing a huge creature with a square, box-like head and massive arms.

2) It's usually described as an ape-like creature over 7 feet tall with large red eyes, long black or reddish-brown hair, and a smell compared to "dead fish, a skunk with bad body odor, decaying peat moss and the musk of a snapping turtle."

Answer: B) Snallygaster

The Snallygaster is said to haunt Frederick County, Maryland, especially South Mountain, Braddock Heights and the Middletown Valley. Its roots go back to the German immigrants who settled the area beginning in the 1730s and told of a monster called a Schneller Geist, meaning "quick ghost." Legend describes it as half bird and half reptile, with a metallic beak lined with razor-sharp teeth and octopus-like tentacles, swooping silently out of the sky to carry off its victims. Seven-pointed stars, said to keep it away, can still be seen painted on local barns. In February and March 1909, newspapers reported a beast with "enormous wings, a long pointed bill, claws like steel hooks, and an eye in the center of its forehead" that screeched "like a locomotive whistle." The Smithsonian Institution reportedly offered a reward for its hide, and President Theodore Roosevelt reportedly considered postponing an African safari to hunt it himself. It later came out that the 1909 reports were a hoax by Middletown Valley Register editor George C. Rhoderick and reporter Ralph S. Wolfe to sell more papers. In 2021, the American Snallygaster Museum opened in Libertytown, Maryland.

Near Keene, North Dakota. October 7, 2026, about 10:55 p.m.

An oil production worker was on night shift, checking on well sites spread out between New Town and Mandaree, the same rounds as every other night. Around 10:55 he pulled onto a well pad and noticed two lights over the next hill, stacked one on top of the other, sitting low, close together and perfectly still above the grassland.

At first he figured it was a new communications tower. But his company's towers carry blue and red lights, and he hadn't seen any new construction out there. Something felt off, so he started recording.

The moment he stopped and reached for his binoculars, the top light started speeding off in his direction, gaining altitude, and a few seconds later it went dark. The lower light held still for another 30 seconds or so, then it sped off and went dark too.

About a minute passed with nothing to see. Then he heard a humming, almost like a vibration. He got out of his vehicle, looked around, and saw a triangle with three lights moving slowly, directly over top of him. No red or green position lights, no flashing beacons, just three solid lights. He recorded again, and when he stopped and looked back up, he could never find it again.

He drove as far as he could on company property toward where the lights had been hovering. He found nothing out of the ordinary, except that the cattle in the pasture were wound up and lively for that time of night. He says he checked FlightRadar, and there were no planes or other aircraft anywhere close.

He filed his report with the National UFO Reporting Center the next day, describing a black triangle listed at 30 by 30 in size, with a haze around it, moving at an estimated 50 to 150 miles per hour. He says he recorded video both times. It's a single witness, and NUFORC hasn't attached any explanation. Drones would be the first ordinary suspect, but the slow pass right overhead, the hum and the missing position lights are the details he made a point of reporting.

New Orleans Square, Disneyland, Anaheim, California. Photographed in 1968, posted August 2026.

Tom Eubank, 84, only wanted to sell his old Canon camera. He'd gotten it in 1963 while serving aboard a Navy ship in the Mediterranean. His granddaughter, Josie Weaver, was helping, and to see what was still on the old film, the two of them tracked down a projector.

Up on the screen came his 1968 trip to Disneyland: the train station, the Swiss Family Treehouse, it's a small world, Pirates of the Caribbean and Sleeping Beauty Castle. And in one shot of New Orleans Square, front and center, stood a man who didn't seem to belong there.

He's wearing a navy blue crewneck T-shirt and modern-looking sunglasses, with a haircut faded on the sides and a square case on a strap over his shoulder, while the guests around him are dressed more formally, in brighter colors. "He looked so different to everyone around him, especially with his haircut," Weaver told People. "It just looked like someone that we would see out and about now."

She posted it to TikTok on August 25 with the caption "found a time traveler in my grandpas film," and it took off, with millions of views and more than a thousand comments. "Bro is from 2010," one wrote. Her grandfather agreed the man looked out of place, but when she suggested a time traveler, he just laughed. Her grandmother was blunter: "These are just old photos."

Plenty of commenters side with Grandma. Sunglasses like his were already around, T-shirts as outerwear had been popular since the 1940s, and one said the case is just a camera bag of the era. Even Weaver hedged in her own caption, noting that Ray-Ban dates back to the 1930s. To this day, nobody has identified the man in the frame.

Newburgh Brewing Company, South Colden Street, Newburgh, New York. October 2026.

The brewery sits in a building that dates to the 1850s. Before the beer, it housed a steam engine operation, a yarn factory and the Newburgh Paper Box Company. In February 2024, owner Paul Halayko put a motion-activated security camera in the kitchen, and it started picking up things he can't explain.

In one frame, a white shape seems to turn into a face. "Kind of like a grimaced mouth right here," he told News 12. "Very creepy with the teeth, definitely see two eyes." Two other overnight recordings caught flashes of light about 47 minutes apart while nobody was inside. Side-by-side stills show pots, a garbage pail, a tray and knives that seem to have moved or vanished. "We've got two knives right there in the middle on the knife rack," he said. "Now let's go to the next photo, they are gone." A worker has also reported seeing a man in overalls several times downstairs in the production area, and describes those encounters as positive.

Halayko asked the city historian whether anyone had ever died in the building. She found no recorded fatal accident, though she warned that industrial work was dangerous and some deaths may never have been written down.

Then, after News 12's first report aired, historian Salvatore LaBruna turned up a New York Times article from January 20, 1867. Two days earlier, a boiler at the Washington Iron Works, an early ironworks tied to the brewery's historic property, blew apart and tore through a brick wall. A 45-year-old worker named Hugh Elwood was thrown against a wall and pinned under the wreckage. Rescuers worked for about an hour to free him, and he died as he was carried out, leaving a wife and four children. A coroner's jury blamed a defective boiler and poor safety precautions. Co-owner Chris Basso says the owners had no idea.

None of the recordings actually show anything moving, and bugs or dust drifting past a motion camera would be the first suspects. Halayko isn't ruling anything out. "I'd be crazy to say it's not possible," he said, "because there are many things in this world that we don't understand."

Ellsworth Air Force Base missile field, near Newell, South Dakota. November 1977.

Mario Woods was a young Air Force security policeman with the 44th Missile Security Squadron, guarding Minuteman II nuclear missiles buried under the western South Dakota prairie. One night in November 1977, he said, he and his partner Michael Johnson answered an alarm at a launch facility called November-5.

Woods said an enormous glowing object was waiting near the site. Intense light came down over their truck, they could barely move, and a smaller dark sphere hung near the vehicle. Then figures approached. The next thing he knew, he was coming to beside a reservoir near Newell, miles away, with hours of his life unaccounted for. Afterward, he said, the two men were separated, questioned and examined, and they lost touch for decades.

He spent most of the next 49 years looking for Johnson. In June 2026 they finally reconnected by phone, and on September 7 the YouTube program American Alchemy published their reunion. Johnson's own waking memories overlap with Woods' on a huge, close light, being unable to move, and a confused aftermath.

On October 16, 2026, just weeks after that reunion, Mario Woods died of leukemia. He was 71.

The debate around his story is real. The missile field, the squadron and the two-man alarm teams all check out, but no duty roster, alarm log or medical record from that night has been published. Much of the detail about beings and procedures surfaced under hypnosis, and the Justice Department warns that memories recovered that way can't be assumed accurate. Even the date gets garbled online: November-5 is the name of the launch site, not the day, and Woods placed the night around November 18. And the best-known 1977 Ellsworth UFO document, a different story entirely, was exposed as a hoax back in 1984.

Whatever happened out there, he carried it for half a century, and he found the one man who could share it with weeks to spare.
